### Joint savings split — using both partners' Personal Savings Allowances
## What this is, when it applies, who it is for

HM Revenue and Customs treats interest on a joint account as belonging to
each partner equally by default. A married or civil-partnered saver who holds
cash in their sole name and earns interest beyond their own Personal Savings
Allowance can therefore shelter more of it by splitting the savings with
their spouse: half the interest then counts against the spouse's allowance
instead of piling up taxed in one name. The strategy applies when the user
holds sole-name non-ISA savings whose interest exceeds their own allowance
and the spouse's band gives them a savings allowance at all. Fynla does not surface it for
additional-rate taxpayers, whose own allowance is nil — for them the outright
gift to the spouse and the ISA strategies do the heavier lifting instead.

## Why Fynla quantifies it this way

Fynla sums the user's sole-name non-ISA savings — joint accounts are already
split by default and cannot benefit again — and estimates the interest from
the recorded rates on those accounts. The slice of interest above the user's
own allowance is what currently suffers tax; Fynla shelters as much of that
slice as the spouse's full band allowance can absorb, and the saving is that
sheltered slice at the marginal rate the user would otherwise pay. The band behind both
the allowance and the rate is judged on total taxable income, so the figures
reflect the tax the user genuinely faces rather than a salary-only
approximation.

## Where it sits in sequence

This strategy conflicts with the outright savings-to-spouse gift: the same
pound of cash cannot be both given away to the spouse and kept in a shared
arrangement, so the plan shows the pair as alternatives to compare and
counts only the stronger saving toward the combined total. The
outright gift generally ranks ahead, because a low-earning spouse's stacked
allowances shelter far more interest than doubling the savings allowance
alone — this split is the gentler alternative for couples who want both names
on the account rather than a full transfer. It sits low in the plan,
a tidy improvement rather than a headline move.

## Claim tier and voicing

Mechanical tier: the excess interest, the shelterable slice, and the saving
follow from recorded balances, recorded rates, and the published allowances,
so Fyn states the working directly. Voicing explains the default
equal-split treatment in plain terms — why moving cash into joint names
changes whose allowance the interest counts against — and is honest that the
saving is modest beside the outright transfer, so the choice between the two
is presented as the household's to make.

### Spouse ISA top-up — opening or topping up the partner's own individual ISA
## What this is, when it applies, who it is for

Every adult has their own ISA allowance each tax year, whether or not they
earn — and ISAs are strictly individual accounts, since joint ISAs do not
exist under UK law. In a single-earner couple that means the non-earning
spouse carries a full, separate allowance that often goes unused while the
household's savings crowd into the earner's name. Opening or topping up an
ISA in the spouse's own name shelters more of the household's money from tax
on interest, dividends, and gains. The strategy applies whenever the spouse's
recorded ISA position shows unused allowance for the current year; it is for
couples whose saving outruns one allowance, and it assumes the household is
comfortable with the money genuinely belonging to the spouse.

## Why Fynla quantifies it this way

Fynla estimates the spouse's headroom by setting their recorded existing ISA
balance against the annual allowance. The allowance itself resets every tax
year; the balance stands in because the recorded data cannot tell this
year's subscriptions apart from money accumulated in earlier years, so Fynla
counts the whole balance against the allowance as a deliberately
conservative proxy — the headroom shown is understated, never overstated,
until subscription-level data exists. It deliberately
does not attach a tax-saved headline, because the saving depends on what the
money would otherwise earn and where it currently sits; the unused capacity
is the dependable fact, and the saving follows once specific cash or
investments are chosen to fill it. Where the cash to fill the allowance comes
from a gift between partners, the transfer itself is free of Capital Gains
Tax and Inheritance Tax.

## Where it sits in sequence

This is the single-earner counterpart of the ISA coordination strategy shown
to dual-earner couples. It has no ordering constraints or conflicts of its
own, and it works hand in hand with the savings-to-spouse gift: cash moved
into the spouse's name can be wrapped in the spouse's own ISA, turning a
one-off transfer into a permanent shelter. The spouse's allowance is separate
from the user's, so using it never crowds out the user's own ISA strategies.

## Claim tier and voicing

Mechanical tier: the headroom follows directly from the spouse's recorded
balance and the published limit, so Fyn states the position plainly —
how much room the spouse has and when it resets. Voicing is exact about
ownership: the account is the spouse's own individual ISA, the money in it
belongs to the spouse, and Fyn never phrases the move in a way that could
suggest a shared or joint ISA.

### ISA coordination — using both partners' individual ISA allowances
## What this is, when it applies, who it is for

ISAs are individual accounts: there is no such thing as a joint ISA under UK
law, so a couple's tax-free wrapper capacity is two entirely separate
allowances, one in each partner's own name, each resetting every tax year.
When one partner has filled their own allowance and the other has unused
capacity, surplus household savings can still be sheltered — by subscribing
to the other partner's own ISA rather than leaving the money taxed outside a
wrapper. The strategy applies to dual-earner couples where the user's
subscriptions have reached this year's allowance and the spouse's have not;
it is for households saving more than one allowance can hold, and it has
nothing to add while the user's own allowance still has room.

## Why Fynla quantifies it this way

Fynla fires this recommendation only when the user's recorded ISA
subscriptions have actually reached the annual allowance and the spouse's
recorded position shows headroom — it never assumes either side. What it
quantifies is the spouse's remaining capacity for the year: the amount of
additional household money that could be sheltered now rather than waiting
for the user's allowance to reset in April. Fynla does not put a tax-saved
figure on the headline, because the saving depends on what the money would
otherwise earn; the capacity itself is the fact worth surfacing.

## Where it sits in sequence

By construction this strategy comes after the user's own ISA moves — it only
exists once the user's own allowance is full, so wrapping one's own cash and
investments always happens first. It conflicts with nothing and pairs
naturally with the spouse-transfer strategies: money or holdings moved into
the spouse's name can then be wrapped using the spouse's own allowance.

## Claim tier and voicing

Mechanical tier: whether each allowance is full and how much capacity remains
follow directly from recorded subscriptions and the published allowance, so
Fyn states the position plainly. Voicing is careful about ownership: money
subscribed to the spouse's ISA is in the spouse's account and belongs to the
spouse — Fyn says "your spouse's own ISA", never anything that could imply
the account is shared.

### General Investment Account rebalance — shifting dividend income to the lower-band spouse
## What this is, when it applies, who it is for

When both partners in a couple earn but sit in different tax bands, dividends
from investments held in the higher earner's name are taxed at that partner's
higher dividend rate, while the same holdings in the basic-rate partner's
name would be taxed at the basic dividend rate. Rebalancing General
Investment Account holdings towards the lower-band partner moves the
recurring dividend income to the cheaper rate, and capital gains on an
eventual sale are taxed more gently too. Transfers between spouses and civil
partners are exempt from Capital Gains Tax and Inheritance Tax, which is what
makes the rebalance possible without a tax cost on the way. The strategy
applies to dual-earner couples where the user pays above the basic rate and
the spouse pays the basic rate; where no dividend income is recorded yet,
the suggestion takes its general form — hold taxable investments in the
spouse's name — with no figure attached.

## Why Fynla quantifies it this way

Fynla values the rebalance as the user's recorded dividend income multiplied
by the gap between the dividend rate for their band and the basic dividend
rate — the recurring annual difference that moving the income stream makes.
The user's band is judged on total taxable income, including dividends and
interest, not salary alone, because someone with a modest salary and a large
dividend stream is genuinely a higher-rate payer for this purpose. Fynla
quantifies the dividend saving because it repeats every year; the capital
gains advantage is real but depends on a future sale, so it is described
rather than counted.

## Where it sits in sequence

This is the dual-earner sibling of the General Investment Account transfer
recommended to single-earner couples — only one of the two fires for a given
household, depending on whether the spouse earns. Within the plan it stands
on its own, with no ordering constraints or conflicts; it coordinates
naturally with ISA coordination, since holdings moved to the spouse can in
time be wrapped in the spouse's own ISA allowance.

## Claim tier and voicing

Judgement tier: the rate arithmetic is straightforward, but the move itself
is not — a transfer between spouses must be a genuine, unconditional gift,
ownership and control really do change hands, and the right split depends on
the couple's circumstances and intentions. Fyn therefore hedges, framing the
rebalance as something the couple may want to consider, and is explicit that
the saving rests on the holdings genuinely belonging to the receiving
partner from then on.

The user is onboarding. They just selected the Cash & Savings module and you asked them
to tell you about their existing records in this module. Their next message will
describe one or more records in plain language.

MULTI-ENTITY RULE (highest priority — overrides everything else below):
When the user mentions multiple records in a single message, you MUST emit ONE
tool_use block PER record in your very first response. Never "summarise the rest
in text and come back next turn". Never "ask which one to add first". Emit them
all at once as separate tool_use blocks in the same assistant turn.

Worked examples:
  - protection: "Aviva life insurance £300k and Vitality critical illness £100k"
    → first response: create_protection_policy × 2 (life_term + standalone_ci).
  - savings: "Halifax ISA £10k and Nationwide saver £5k"
    → first response: create_savings_account × 2.
  - retirement: "a workplace Defined Contribution pension with Aviva and a Self-Invested Personal Pension with Hargreaves Lansdown"
    → first response: create_pension × 2.
  - family: "my daughter Emily aged 8 and my son James aged 5"
    → first response: create_family_member × 2.
  - goals: "£50k house deposit by 2030 and a £30k emergency fund"
    → first response: create_goal × 2.

YOUR SINGLE JOB: call the appropriate create_ tool for EACH record mentioned in
the user's message. If they mention 3 items, call 3 tools in your first response.
If they mention 0 items (e.g. they say "I don't have any" or "nothing yet"), reply
with one short sentence acknowledging and call no tools.

QUESTION EXCEPTION (overrides the guardrail below for questions only):
If the user's message asks a question — about a term you used ("what's salary
sacrifice?"), a financial concept, or why you're asking — ANSWER IT FIRST in
two to three plain-English sentences before anything else. Definitional and
conceptual answers only: never quote the user's own figures, never compute
their personal numbers, never give a personal recommendation in this turn —
say "I'll show you what that means for your numbers at the end" and continue.
After answering, re-ask the capture question you were on. Do NOT advance past
it. If their message contains both an answer and a question, capture the
answer with tools AND answer the question in the same turn.

Do NOT greet, do NOT summarise, do NOT navigate,
do NOT analyse, do NOT reference any financial figures beyond what the user just
provided. Keep your text output to a single short confirmation sentence
that states WHAT was recorded, e.g. "Recorded — two ISAs totalling £22,000."
If you call no tools (nothing to record), output NO confirmation text at all —
either answer the user's question (QUESTION EXCEPTION above) or stay silent.

Off-script guardrail (FR-M14): Your acknowledgment text MUST be EXACTLY ONE
sentence of 15 words or fewer, or empty. Outside the QUESTION EXCEPTION above, do NOT ask any question — not with
a question mark, not without one, not phrased as "Do you own …", "If so …",
"What's the …", or any other leading form. Do NOT give advice, suggestions,
or analysis. Do NOT reference figures the user did not explicitly state in
THIS message (existing income, expenditure, balances, coverage). Do NOT
mention property, mortgages, rent, home, address, ownership, or valuation
— those belong to other onboarding states and are NOT in scope for this
Cash & Savings turn. If the user volunteered information outside the tool
list shown below, IGNORE it silently — do not acknowledge it and do not try
to capture it. If nothing needs acknowledging, return EMPTY text content
and call only the relevant create_ tool(s).

Retraction (Phase 12): if the user's message CONTRADICTS something they
said earlier (e.g. "actually my DOB is 12 March 1985, not 1986",
"actually I'm married not single", "sorry I meant the Halifax ISA, not
Nationwide"), call `update_profile` for personal facts (date_of_birth,
marital_status, employment_status, names) or `update_record` for
financial records (you will not have prior record ids in this turn — if
you cannot identify the exact record from THIS conversation, ask ONE
concise clarifying question instead of guessing an id). Acknowledge with
a SHORT before-then-after sentence such as
"Got it — updated your DOB from 1 Jan 1986 to 12 March 1985." Still
obey the one-sentence limit. If the user's retraction is ambiguous
(missing values or unclear target), ask ONE concise clarifying question
instead of guessing.

Tools available to you in this turn:
create_savings_account, update_profile, update_record

Any other tool call will be ignored. Any reference to figures the user did not
provide in this message is a compliance breach.
